claim: ChR2 was expressed in DA neurons by injecting an adeno-associated virus containing FLEX-ChR2 into DAT-Cre transgenic mice.
source: To identify neurons, we expressed the light-gated cation channel, channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), in DA and GABA neurons by injecting an adeno-associated virus containing FLEX-ChR2 into DAT-Cre and VGAT-Cre transgenic mice, respectively (Bäckman et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2009; Vong et al., 2011; Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure used to express ChR2 in specific neuronal populations.

claim: ChR2 was expressed in GABA neurons by injecting an adeno-associated virus containing FLEX-ChR2 into VGAT-Cre transgenic mice.
source: To identify neurons, we expressed the light-gated cation channel, channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), in DA and GABA neurons by injecting an adeno-associated virus containing FLEX-ChR2 into DAT-Cre and VGAT-Cre transgenic mice, respectively (Bäckman et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2009; Vong et al., 2011; Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure used to express ChR2 in specific neuronal populations.

claim: 104 DA neurons were identified with significant excitatory responses to light pulses from five DAT-Cre mice.
source: We identified 104 neurons recorded from five DAT-Cre mice (hereafter referred to as DA neurons) and 74 neurons recorded from four VGAT-Cre mice (GABA neurons) with significant excitatory responses to light pulses (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of neurons identified through optogenetic stimulation.

claim: 74 GABA neurons were identified with significant excitatory responses to light pulses from four VGAT-Cre mice.
source: We identified 104 neurons recorded from five DAT-Cre mice (hereafter referred to as DA neurons) and 74 neurons recorded from four VGAT-Cre mice (GABA neurons) with significant excitatory responses to light pulses (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of neurons identified through optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Light-induced spikes from identified neurons were almost identical to spontaneous spikes with waveform correlation coefficient >0.9.
source: Light-induced spikes from these neurons were almost identical to spontaneous spikes (waveform correlation coefficient >0.9, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of spike waveform similarity.

claim: DA neurons fired action potentials with wider waveforms than GABA neurons.
source: In addition, the electrophysiological profiles of the identified neuronal populations resembled those of previous studies (i.e. DA neurons fired action potentials with both wider waveforms and slower spontaneous firing rates than GABA neurons; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirming the selective expression of ChR2 in DA and GABA neurons (Cohen et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological characteristics of identified neurons and cites previous studies.

claim: DA neurons fired action potentials with slower spontaneous firing rates than GABA neurons.
source: In addition, the electrophysiological profiles of the identified neuronal populations resembled those of previous studies (i.e. DA neurons fired action potentials with both wider waveforms and slower spontaneous firing rates than GABA neurons; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirming the selective expression of ChR2 in DA and GABA neurons (Cohen et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological characteristics of identified neurons and cites previous studies.

claim: The total correct performance rate in the memory task was 86.8 ± 7.9% averaged across sessions.
source: Averaging across sessions, the total correct rate was 86.8 ± 7.9% (mean ± standard deviation [SD]; left: 88.1 ± 10.0%, right: 87.2 ± 11.6%; paired t-test evaluating left vs right performance rate: t(59) = 0.46, p=0.65, 60 sessions in nine mice, Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral performance data with statistical measures.

claim: There was no significant difference between left and right trial performance rates in the memory task.
source: Averaging across sessions, the total correct rate was 86.8 ± 7.9% (mean ± standard deviation [SD]; left: 88.1 ± 10.0%, right: 87.2 ± 11.6%; paired t-test evaluating left vs right performance rate: t(59) = 0.46, p=0.65, 60 sessions in nine mice, Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing performance rates.

claim: Performance was independent of individual preference for left-or-right arm visits in any of the recorded sessions.
source: In addition, performance was independent of individual preference for the left-or-right arm visits in any of the recorded sessions (test of independence, χ2(1)<3.84, p>0.05, Ho: correct rate is independent of arm choice, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results for independence of performance and arm choice.

claim: Correct performance rate dropped with higher memory load demands.
source: Across all sessions, the correct performance rate dropped with higher memory load demands (mean ± SD; low load: 83.1 ± 8.3%, high load: 73.9 ± 9.5%; paired t-test on correct performance rate: t(12) = 4.33, p<0.001, 13 sessions in seven mice, Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral performance data under different memory load conditions with statistical analysis.

claim: The average discharge rate of identified DA neurons remained essentially constant throughout trials.
source: Corroborating these earlier reports, the average discharge rate of identified DA neurons in the present study remained essentially constant (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the population activity pattern of DA neurons.

claim: From the beginning until the end of the trial, the population activity of DA neurons deviated slightly by 0.17±0.62 Hz.
source: Simple linear regression analysis, with the neuronal firing rate as the response variable and the animal's position on the maze as the single predictor variable, showed that from the beginning until the end of the trial (a 1.5-m distance), the population activity of DA neurons deviated slightly by 0.17±0.62 Hz (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], did not differ from a distribution with a mean equal to zero; one-sample t-test on the position coefficient, t(103) = 0.275, p=0.78).
evidence: The manuscript reports regression analysis results on DA neuron population activity.

claim: In the memory-delay period, the discharge rate of DA neurons declined by -0.72±2.3 Hz.
source: Notably, in the memory-delay period, the discharge rate of DA neurons declined by - 0.72±2.3 Hz (mean ± SEM, one-sample t-test on the position coefficient, t(103) = –0.31, p=0.75).
evidence: The manuscript reports regression analysis results on DA neuron activity during memory delay.

claim: GABA neurons elevated their discharge rate by 4.29 ± 1.10 Hz in the delay period.
source: On the other hand, the GABA neurons elevated their discharge rate by 4.29 ± 1.10 Hz in the delay period (mean ± SEM, one-sample t-test on the position coefficient, t(73) = 4.09, p<0.001), confirming evidence from an earlier report (Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports regression analysis results on GABA neuron activity during memory delay and cites a previous study.

claim: Approximately 21% of DA neurons differentiated their response between left or right trajectories in the delay section.
source: Almost 20% of DA neurons differentiated their response between left or right trajectories in those maze sections (21% in the delay section and 22% in the side-arm section, 104 neurons, permutation test, p<0.05, Figure 3B and Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of neurons showing trajectory-specific activity based on permutation test results.

claim: Approximately 22% of DA neurons differentiated their response between left or right trajectories in the side-arm section.
source: Almost 20% of DA neurons differentiated their response between left or right trajectories in those maze sections (21% in the delay section and 22% in the side-arm section, 104 neurons, permutation test, p<0.05, Figure 3B and Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of neurons showing trajectory-specific activity based on permutation test results.

claim: Approximately 47% of GABA neurons differentiated their response between left or right trajectories in the delay section.
source: In GABA neurons, the percentage was even higher, with almost 50% of these cells eliciting trajectory-specific activities (47% in the delay section and 47% in the side-arm section, 74 neurons, permutation test, p<0.05, Figure 3B and Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of neurons showing trajectory-specific activity based on permutation test results.

claim: Approximately 47% of GABA neurons differentiated their response between left or right trajectories in the side-arm section.
source: In GABA neurons, the percentage was even higher, with almost 50% of these cells eliciting trajectory-specific activities (47% in the delay section and 47% in the side-arm section, 74 neurons, permutation test, p<0.05, Figure 3B and Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of neurons showing trajectory-specific activity based on permutation test results.

claim: Multiple regression analysis showed that all examined variables (lap trajectory, trial number, speed, trial accuracy, and reward history) contributed to the firing activities of neuronal subpopulations.
source: We found that all the examined variables (lap trajectory, trial number, speed, trial accuracy, and reward history) contributed to the firing activities of neuronal subpopulations; however, only the lap trajectory predictor could explain better the trajectory-specific activities observed in the ~20% of DA and ~50% of GABA neurons that were identified with the permutation analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from multiple regression analysis.

claim: Only the lap trajectory predictor could explain better the trajectory-specific activities observed in ~20% of DA and ~50% of GABA neurons.
source: We found that all the examined variables (lap trajectory, trial number, speed, trial accuracy, and reward history) contributed to the firing activities of neuronal subpopulations; however, only the lap trajectory predictor could explain better the trajectory-specific activities observed in the ~20% of DA and ~50% of GABA neurons that were identified with the permutation analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from multiple regression analysis comparing different predictors.

claim: In the delay section of the no-cue-no-choice task, there was a significant reduction in the number of positions with a significant firing rate difference for DA neurons compared to the memory task.
source: In the delay section of the no-cue-no-choice task, we observed a significant reduction in the number of positions with a significant firing rate difference (mean ± SD; DA: memory task 5.9±3.8 points, no-cue-no-choice task 1.5 ± 3.4 points, paired t-test, p=0.002, four animals; GABA: memory task 10.7 ± 3.9 points, no-cue-no-choice task 1.5 ± 2.0 points, paired t-test, p<0.001, three animals, Figure 4B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences between tasks.

claim: In the delay section of the no-cue-no-choice task, there was a significant reduction in the number of positions with a significant firing rate difference for GABA neurons compared to the memory task.
source: In the delay section of the no-cue-no-choice task, we observed a significant reduction in the number of positions with a significant firing rate difference (mean ± SD; DA: memory task 5.9±3.8 points, no-cue-no-choice task 1.5 ± 3.4 points, paired t-test, p=0.002, four animals; GABA: memory task 10.7 ± 3.9 points, no-cue-no-choice task 1.5 ± 2.0 points, paired t-test, p<0.001, three animals, Figure 4B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences between tasks.

claim: The firing rate difference between left and right-side arms was strong in both memory task and no-cue-no-choice task for DA neurons.
source: However, the firing rate difference between the left and right-side arms was strong in both tasks (DA: memory task 8.5 ± 7.8 points, no-cue-no-choice task 5.9±7.4 points, paired t-test, p=0.139, four animals; GABA: memory task 12.6±8.1 points, no-cue-no-choice task 9.9±8.8 points, paired t-test, p=0.234, three animals, Figure 4B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences in side arms between tasks.

claim: The firing rate difference between left and right-side arms was strong in both memory task and no-cue-no-choice task for GABA neurons.
source: However, the firing rate difference between the left and right-side arms was strong in both tasks (DA: memory task 8.5 ± 7.8 points, no-cue-no-choice task 5.9±7.4 points, paired t-test, p=0.139, four animals; GABA: memory task 12.6±8.1 points, no-cue-no-choice task 9.9±8.8 points, paired t-test, p=0.234, three animals, Figure 4B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences in side arms between tasks.

claim: In the delay section of the cue-no-choice task, there was a significant reduction in the spatial extent of the firing rate difference for DA neurons compared to the memory task.
source: Similar to the first control task, in the delay section of the cue-no-choice task we observed a significant reduction in the spatial extent of the firing rate difference (DA: memory task 5.4±3.6 points, cue-no-choice task: 0.4±1.1, paired t-test, p=0.011, four animals; GABA: memory task 10.7±6.3 points, cue-no-choice task 3.5±4.2 points, paired t-test, p<0.001, 1 animal, Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences between tasks.

claim: In the delay section of the cue-no-choice task, there was a significant reduction in the spatial extent of the firing rate difference for GABA neurons compared to the memory task.
source: Similar to the first control task, in the delay section of the cue-no-choice task we observed a significant reduction in the spatial extent of the firing rate difference (DA: memory task 5.4±3.6 points, cue-no-choice task: 0.4±1.1, paired t-test, p=0.011, four animals; GABA: memory task 10.7±6.3 points, cue-no-choice task 3.5±4.2 points, paired t-test, p<0.001, 1 animal, Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences between tasks.

claim: In the side arms, the trajectory-specific effect remained strong and was not significantly different from the effect observed in the memory task for DA neurons.
source: In the side arms, however, the trajectory-specific effect remained strong and was not significantly different from the effect observed in the memory task (DA: memory task 8.1±10.3 points, cue-no-choice task 5.0±4.6 points, paired t-test, p=0.146, four animals; GABA: memory task 8.7±5.9 points, cue-no-choice 5.2±6.2 points, paired t-test, p=0.086, 1 animal, Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences in side arms between tasks.

claim: In the side arms, the trajectory-specific effect remained strong and was not significantly different from the effect observed in the memory task for GABA neurons.
source: In the side arms, however, the trajectory-specific effect remained strong and was not significantly different from the effect observed in the memory task (DA: memory task 8.1±10.3 points, cue-no-choice task 5.0±4.6 points, paired t-test, p=0.146, four animals; GABA: memory task 8.7±5.9 points, cue-no-choice 5.2±6.2 points, paired t-test, p=0.086, 1 animal, Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rate differences in side arms between tasks.

claim: 27 DA neurons (28% of 104 neurons) responded to reward with significant excitation.
source: In agreement with this notion, we discovered that 27 DA neurons (28% of 104 neurons, Figure 6B column 4; we defined the first second of reward consumption as the reward section.) responded to reward with significant excitation.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of neurons showing reward-related excitation.

claim: 23% of DA neurons differed significantly in their responses to left-or-right rewards.
source: However, we found that 23% of DA neurons and 46% of GABA neurons differed significantly in their responses to left-or-right rewards (Figure 6A and B column 3, and Table 1; paired t-test comparing mean firing rates, p<0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of neurons showing differential reward responses.

claim: 46% of GABA neurons differed significantly in their responses to left-or-right rewards.
source: However, we found that 23% of DA neurons and 46% of GABA neurons differed significantly in their responses to left-or-right rewards (Figure 6A and B column 3, and Table 1; paired t-test comparing mean firing rates, p<0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of neurons showing differential reward responses.

claim: In both DA and GABA neuronal populations, there was a significant positive relationship between the reward and side-arm sections in firing rate differences.
source: In both neuronal populations, we found a significant positive relationship between the reward and side-arm sections (Figure 6C; Pearson's correlation; DA: R=0.31, p<0.001; GABA: R=0.67, p<0.001) but not between the reward and delay sections (Figure 6C; Pearson's correlation; DA: R=–0.05, p>0.05; GABA: R=–0.03, p>0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results between different maze sections.

claim: There was no significant relationship between the reward and delay sections in firing rate differences for DA and GABA neurons.
source: In both neuronal populations, we found a significant positive relationship between the reward and side-arm sections (Figure 6C; Pearson's correlation; DA: R=0.31, p<0.001; GABA: R=0.67, p<0.001) but not between the reward and delay sections (Figure 6C; Pearson's correlation; DA: R=–0.05, p>0.05; GABA: R=–0.03, p>0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results between different maze sections.

claim: Only four DA neurons showed the same side preference in the reward and delay sections.
source: We discovered that only four (n=4 out of 104) DA neurons showed the same side preference in the reward and delay sections (e.g. elicit significantly stronger firing activities in the delay section of left trials and left reward).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of neurons showing consistent trajectory preference across maze sections.

claim: Trajectory-specific GABA neurons were located more laterally compared to the rest of the GABA population.
source: Estimating the location of recorded neurons (i.e. Bregma vs Mediolateral coordinates) from the anatomical reconstruction of the recording channels revealed that the trajectory-specific GABA neurons were located more laterally compared to the rest of the group (Bregma: t(72) = 1.165, p=0.248, Mediolateral: t(72) = –2.38, p=0.019, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports anatomical analysis results with statistical tests.

claim: In DA neurons there was no clear anatomical segregation between trajectory-specific and non-trajectory-specific neurons.
source: However, in the DA neurons there was no clear anatomical segregation (Bregma: t(102) = 0.045, p=0.964, Mediolateral: t(102) = 0.177, p=0.860, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports anatomical analysis results with statistical tests.

claim: The midbrain dopamine system plays a crucial role in higher cognitive functions, including updating and maintaining short-term memory.
source: Although the midbrain dopamine (DA) system plays a crucial role in higher cognitive functions, including updating and maintaining short-term memory, the encoding properties of the somatic spiking activity of ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons for short-term memory computations have not yet been identified.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The encoding properties of the somatic spiking activity of VTA DA neurons for short-term memory computations have not yet been identified.
source: Although the midbrain dopamine (DA) system plays a crucial role in higher cognitive functions, including updating and maintaining short-term memory, the encoding properties of the somatic spiking activity of ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons for short-term memory computations have not yet been identified.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Trajectory-specific responses in the delay period of the memory task could reflect short-term memory representations linked to decision-making behavior.
source: Together, these results suggest that trajectory-specific responses in the delay period of the memory task could reflect short-term memory representations linked to decision-making behavior and cannot be explained by running speed, motor, and motivation-related signaling differences.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the control task experiments.

claim: Trajectory-specific responses in the delay period cannot be explained by running speed, motor, and motivation-related signaling differences.
source: Together, these results suggest that trajectory-specific responses in the delay period of the memory task could reflect short-term memory representations linked to decision-making behavior and cannot be explained by running speed, motor, and motivation-related signaling differences.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the control task experiments.

claim: DA neurons originating in the VTA project to diverse forebrain regions, forming distinct but interacting neuromodulatory systems.
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons originating in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) project to diverse forebrain regions, forming distinct but interacting neuromodulatory systems that are thought to play pivotal roles in the regulation of reward-related learning, motivation, and cognition (Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Schultz et al., 1993; Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Schultz et al., 1997; Tzschentke, 2001; Schultz, 2002; Pierce and Kumaresan, 2006; Berridge, 2007; Vijayraghavan et al., 2007; Lammel et al., 2008; Robbins and Arnsten, 2009; Hauber, 2010; Cohen et al., 2012; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Howe et al., 2013; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013; Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this established knowledge.

claim: VTA DA neurons play pivotal roles in the regulation of reward-related learning, motivation, and cognition.
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons originating in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) project to diverse forebrain regions, forming distinct but interacting neuromodulatory systems that are thought to play pivotal roles in the regulation of reward-related learning, motivation, and cognition (Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Schultz et al., 1993; Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Schultz et al., 1997; Tzschentke, 2001; Schultz, 2002; Pierce and Kumaresan, 2006; Berridge, 2007; Vijayraghavan et al., 2007; Lammel et al., 2008; Robbins and Arnsten, 2009; Hauber, 2010; Cohen et al., 2012; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Howe et al., 2013; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013; Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this established knowledge.

claim: Midbrain DA activity promotes behaviors associated with motivation.
source: A wealth of electrophysiological recordings from midbrain DA neurons, complemented by in vivo microdialysis data indicate that midbrain DA activity promotes behaviors associated with motivation (Wise, 2004; Berridge, 2007; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Howe et al., 2013; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013; Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019) and supports reward-based learning by encoding reward prediction error (RPE) signals (Schultz et al., 1993; Schultz et al., 1997; Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: Midbrain DA activity supports reward-based learning by encoding reward prediction error (RPE) signals.
source: A wealth of electrophysiological recordings from midbrain DA neurons, complemented by in vivo microdialysis data indicate that midbrain DA activity promotes behaviors associated with motivation (Wise, 2004; Berridge, 2007; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Howe et al., 2013; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013; Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019) and supports reward-based learning by encoding reward prediction error (RPE) signals (Schultz et al., 1993; Schultz et al., 1997; Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: DA is of central importance to higher cognitive functions, such as updating and maintaining short-term memory.
source: Also, DA is of central importance to higher cognitive functions, such as updating and maintaining short-term memory (Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Ott and Nieder, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this established knowledge.

claim: An inverted-U-shape effect was discovered, where too little or too much DA receptor stimulation impairs PFC-engaging short-term memory.
source: An inverted-U-shape effect was discovered, where too little or too much DA receptor stimulation impairs PFC-engaging short-term memory (Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Vijayraghavan et al., 2007; Robbins and Arnsten, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies that discovered this effect.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings at the VTA showed that DA neurons are not active in the delay period of memory tasks.
source: Moreover, at the origin of the DA system, electrophysiological recordings at the VTA showed that DA neurons are not active in the delay period of memory tasks (Schultz et al., 1993; Schultz, 2002; Phillips et al., 2004; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013; Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies reporting this finding.

claim: The 'gating theory' provides a unified computational framework for reward prediction and short-term memory.
source: They proposed the 'gating theory', which provided a unified computational framework for reward prediction and short-term memory (Cohen et al., 2002; Dreher and Burnod, 2002; Montague et al., 2004; Ott and Nieder, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies that proposed this theory.

claim: According to the gating theory, reward-predicting cues elicit phasic DA release which opens the gate for afferent signals to be stored in memory.
source: According to the model, reward-predicting cues, elicit phasic DA release which opens the gate for the afferent signals to be stored in memory (update).
evidence: The manuscript describes the gating theory model.

claim: According to the gating theory, in the delay period, low, tonic DA levels close the gate for interfering signals to enter the PFC and overwrite the short-term memory component.
source: But, in the delay period, low, tonic DA levels close the gate for interfering signals to enter the PFC and overwrite the short-term memory component (maintenance).
evidence: The manuscript describes the gating theory model.

claim: Persistent neuronal activity might not be the only candidate mechanism for the active maintenance of goal representation over short delays.
source: However, recent advances in the study of the brain's functional organization suggest that persistent neuronal activity might not be the only candidate mechanism for the active maintenance of goal representation over short delays, leading to the proposal of new coding schemes for short-term memory (Stokes, 2015; Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies proposing alternative mechanisms.

claim: Neural oscillations are thought to offer the networking framework for the temporal organization of neuronal activity and information processing in short-term memory.
source: Neural oscillations are abundant in the mammalian brain and are thought to offer the networking framework for the temporal organization of neuronal activity and information processing in short-term memory (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2006; Buschman et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this theoretical framework.

claim: The VTA engages dynamically in the large-scale network of brain systems that support memory-related information processing.
source: Among other basal ganglia regions, the VTA engages dynamically in the large-scale network of brain systems that support memory-related information processing.
evidence: The manuscript states this based on cited research.

claim: Neural oscillations (4 Hz) were prominent in both PFC and VTA throughout the T-maze task, but their power and coherence were adaptively increased in memory delay.
source: Simultaneous electrophysiological recordings were performed in the PFC and the VTA while rodents executed memory-guided behavioral choices in a T-maze task (Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011). Neural oscillations (4 Hz) were prominent in both regions throughout the task, but their power and coherence were adaptively increased in memory delay.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study reporting these findings.

claim: PFC and parietal neurons differentiate their firing activities between opposite behavioral choices while rodents navigate the maze performing memory-guided decisions.
source: In a similar behavioral task, another short-term memory-related coding scheme was reported, this time at the single neuronal level. It was shown that while rodents navigate the maze, performing memory-guided decisions, PFC and parietal neurons differentiate their firing activities between opposite behavioral choices (Fujisawa et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies reporting these findings.

claim: Neurons utilizing GABA as a neurotransmitter constitute approximately 30% of the VTA neuronal population.
source: Neurons utilizing GABA as a neurotransmitter constitute approximately 30% of the VTA neuronal population.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge.

claim: There is evidence of a strong inhibitory influence of VTA GABA neurons on neighboring DA neurons.
source: The memory-related encoding properties of these inhibitory neurons have been largely overlooked, despite evidence of a strong inhibitory influence on neighboring DA neurons (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2009; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012) and well-established interconnections with the PFC circuit (Carr and Sesack, 2000a; Carr and Sesack, 2000b).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies demonstrating this inhibitory influence.

claim: VTA GABA neurons have well-established interconnections with the PFC circuit.
source: The memory-related encoding properties of these inhibitory neurons have been largely overlooked, despite evidence of a strong inhibitory influence on neighboring DA neurons (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2009; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012) and well-established interconnections with the PFC circuit (Carr and Sesack, 2000a; Carr and Sesack, 2000b).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies demonstrating these connections.

claim: Field potentials stem mainly from phase-aligned excitatory or inhibitory post-synaptic potentials, whereas spiking activity is sparse.
source: We took into consideration that (i) earlier studies analyzed either the activity of putative DA neurons or drew inferences of the population activity from voltammetry and fiber photometry recordings (Schultz et al., 1993; Schultz, 2002; Phillips et al., 2004; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013; Choi et al., 2020), and (ii) field potentials (like the 4 Hz oscillations recorded in the VTA) stem mainly from phase-aligned excitatory or inhibitory post-synaptic potentials, whereas spiking activity is sparse (Traub et al., 2004; Buzsáki, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this neurophysiological principle.

claim: A recent report revealed the causal relationship of DA activity with short-term memory by inhibiting DA neurons with optogenetic tools.
source: (iii) A recent report revealed the causal relationship of DA activity with short-term memory, by inhibiting DA neurons with optogenetic tools. However, they did not report the encoding properties of single VTA DA neurons (Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study demonstrating this causal relationship.

claim: Subpopulations of DA and GABA neurons encode internally generated signals that support short-term memory in decision-making.
source: This evidence indicates that populations of DA and GABA neurons in the VTA encode internally generated signals that support short-term memory in decision-making.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: DA neurons are functionally and genetically segregated.
source: However, a wealth of recent studies has shown that DA neurons are functionally and genetically segregated (Lammel et al., 2008; Lammel et al., 2011; Engelhard et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies demonstrating this segregation.

claim: Memory-specific activities by midbrain DA neurons can be represented as trajectory-specific responses in the delay period of the memory task.
source: Here, we demonstrated that memory-specific activities by midbrain DA neurons can be represented as trajectory-specific responses in the delay period of the memory task.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Motor preparation coding schemes for left or right arm responses cannot account for the trajectory-specific activities in the memory delay of the T-maze task.
source: We tested this theory, but we found that the firing rate differences between left and right-arm responses declined in a control behavioral task (cue-no-choice) without memory load but with the same motor skill requirements as the memory task. From this, we concluded that motor preparation coding schemes for left or right arm responses (Cohen et al., 2002; Ott and Nieder, 2019) cannot account for the trajectory-specific activities in the memory delay of the T-maze task.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from control task experiments.

claim: Trajectory-specific activities by DA and GABA neurons are functionally linked to the maintaining and manipulating of memory contents.
source: Instead, our evidence indicates that trajectory-specific activities by DA (also GABA) neurons are functionally linked to the maintaining and manipulating of memory contents.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The memory-related, trajectory-specific midbrain neuronal activities have also been reported for PFC and post-parietal neurons while rodents perform reward-seeking responses on the T-maze.

source: There are reports demonstrating that GABA neurons of the VTA suppress reward consummatory behavior (van Zessen et al., 2012), facilitate aversive behavior (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; Tan et al., 2012), and elicit sustained activities in the delay period between conditioned and unconditioned stimuli (Cohen et al., 2012).

claim: Dendritic inhibition is not as strong as somatic inhibition.
source: Although potent and well-suited for coordinated network activity, this synaptic inhibition is not as strong as somatic inhibition (Jhou et al., 2009; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2009), and it has been suggested that it is not sufficient to suppress DA neurons when they receive a strong excitatory drive from extrinsic sources (van Zessen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this neurophysiological principle.

claim: Dendritic inhibition is not sufficient to suppress DA neurons when they receive a strong excitatory drive from extrinsic sources.

claim: Evidence from the prefrontal cortex and hippocampal formation demonstrates that the excitation of the local network of inhibitory neurons is crucial for the generation and maintenance of network oscillations.
